<div class="mod-meta">Contributors: Michele Dolce · Status: skeleton</div>
{{Discuss|channel=examples}}

The Couette flow is the linear shear <math display="inline">u=(y,0)</math>, considered here in the simplest possible domain for this problem, <math display="inline">(x,y)\in\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}</math>. The equation under study then reduces to
<math display="block">\partial_t f+y\partial_xf=\nu\Delta f, \qquad f|_{t=0}=f^{\rm in}, \qquad (x,y)\in \mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}.</math>
This is a foundational model in the field, because the same equation governs the vorticity of the two-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations linearized around the Couette flow. In that context Kelvin already solved it explicitly in 1887 (see [[Literature#Kelvin1887|Kelvin (1887, eq. (34)–(35))]]). Moreover, the same model, without the diffusion in <math display="inline">x</math>, was derived by [[Literature#Kolmogorov1934|Kolmogorov (1934)]] when developing his theory of Brownian motion, and the equation is also of Fokker–Planck type. See also [[History of the problem]].

We use this model to illustrate what typical mixing and enhanced dissipation results look like, and how the two are related. The model is simple enough that each proof technique can be carried out in full. They are all presented below on this single example.

{{Fold start|kind=note|title=Why this domain?}}
The domain <math display="inline">\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}</math> is mathematically convenient: there are no boundaries, and one can take the Fourier transform in both variables.

There is also a more geometric motivation. Consider a circular flow in the plane, <math display="inline">u=rV(r)e_\theta</math>, for which the equation reads <math display="inline">\partial_tf+V(r)\partial_\theta f=\nu\Delta f</math>. The log-polar coordinates <math display="inline">X=e^s\cos(\theta)</math>, <math display="inline">Y=e^s\sin(\theta)</math> identify <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}</math> with <math display="inline">(\theta,s)\in\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}</math>, as shown in the figure below.

{{Media|kind=image|file=log-polar-map.svg|caption=Left: the plane, with two annuli of the same width and a ray (dashed) carried by a circular flow for some time (solid). Right: the same picture in log-polar coordinates. The annuli become strips, and the circular flow becomes a shear flow.}}

Note that this is a conformal change of variables, so the Laplacian only gains a scalar factor, and the equation becomes
<math display="block">\partial_t f+V(e^s)\partial_\theta f=\nu e^{-2s}(\partial_\theta^2+\partial_s^2)f,\qquad (\theta,s)\in\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}.</math>
If we localize near a radius <math display="inline">r_0=e^{s_0}</math> where <math display="inline">V'(r_0)\neq0</math>, then to leading order, and up to constants, we recover the equation for the Couette flow. In this sense, the Couette flow can be seen as a first local approximation of a radial vortex in <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^2</math>, in a region where the angular velocity is strictly monotone. Below is a video showing the effect of the conformal mapping.

{{Media|kind=video|file=log-polar.mp4|poster=log-polar-poster.png|caption=Left: a scalar transported and diffused by the circular flow with <math display="inline">V(r)=1/(1+r^2)</math>. Right: the same solution in log-polar coordinates, where the flow is a shear flow.|record=num-log-polar}}
{{Fold end}}

== The result ==
Before introducing the main theorem, it is useful to observe that, taking the <math display="inline">x</math>-average, one is left with the standard heat equation on <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}</math>. Namely,
<math display="block">\langle f\rangle_x=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{T}}f(x,y)\,dx\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle f(t)\rangle_x=e^{\nu t\partial_{yy}}\langle f^{\rm in}\rangle_x.</math>
For this part of the solution there is therefore nothing new to say, and it enjoys the standard diffusive estimates. Hence, the quantity to measure is how fast the solution approaches its <math display="inline">x</math>-average.

{{Theorem start|id=thm-couette|title=Theorem.}}
Let <math display="inline">\nu\in[0,1)</math> and let <math display="inline">f</math> be the solution with initial datum <math display="inline">f^{\rm in}\in L^2(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})</math>. There exist constants <math display="inline">c,C>0</math>, independent of <math display="inline">\nu</math>, such that for all <math display="inline">t\geq0</math> the following inequality holds true:
<math display="block">\|(f-\langle f\rangle_x)(t)\|_{L^2}\leq Ce^{-c\nu^{1/3}t}\|f^{\rm in}-\langle f^{\rm in}\rangle_x\|_{L^2}.</math>
Moreover, if <math display="inline">f^{\rm in}\in H^1(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})</math>, the following mixing estimate, uniform in <math display="inline">\nu</math>, holds true:
<math display="block">\|(f-\langle f\rangle_x)(t)\|_{H^{-1}}\leq\frac{C}{1+t}e^{-c\nu^{1/3}t}\|f^{\rm in}-\langle f^{\rm in}\rangle_x\|_{H^1}.</math>
{{Theorem end}}
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=The x-average as a projection}}
The <math display="inline">x</math>-average is in fact nothing more than the orthogonal projection in <math display="inline">L^2</math> onto the kernel of the transport operator <math display="inline">y\partial_x</math>: the functions in the kernel are exactly those that do not depend on <math display="inline">x</math>. When the transport operator has a non-trivial kernel, we cannot expect the elements of the kernel to experience any mixing at all from the transport. The interaction with the dissipation is however much more subtle, and it relies heavily on the commutation properties of this projection with the diffusion operator. In this very simple case everything trivializes: the projection commutes with <math display="inline">\nu\Delta</math>, so the <math display="inline">x</math>-average solves the heat equation and <math display="inline">f-\langle f\rangle_x</math> solves the same equation as <math display="inline">f</math>. But the mathematical structure behind the convergence towards the <math display="inline">x</math>-average lies in the fact that the transport operator has a non-trivial kernel.
{{Fold end}}
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=Why negative Sobolev norms measure mixing}}
The <math display="inline">L^2</math> norm does not see mixing: for <math display="inline">\nu=0</math> it is conserved, whatever the flow does. The norm of <math display="inline">H^{-1}</math> does, because it measures how much of a function has been sent to high frequencies: in Fourier, it weighs each mode by the inverse of the size of its frequency, so it is small when the function lives at high frequencies, even if its <math display="inline">L^2</math> norm is not. On the physical side, negative Sobolev norms scale as powers of a length: the ratio <math display="inline">\|g\|_{H^{-1}}/\|g\|_{L^2}</math> can be thought of as the length at which <math display="inline">g</math> oscillates. For <math display="inline">\nu=0</math>, the theorem says that this length decays like <math display="inline">1/t</math>. See also the note on mixing in the [[Overview]].
{{Fold end}}
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=Other function spaces}}
The theorem is stated in spaces based on <math display="inline">L^2</math>. Since the flow is incompressible, the equation does not increase any <math display="inline">L^p</math> norm. For <math display="inline">1<p<\infty</math>, enhanced dissipation in <math display="inline">L^p</math> then follows from the <math display="inline">L^2</math> estimate by interpolation, with a rate that degenerates as <math display="inline">p\to1</math> and as <math display="inline">p\to\infty</math>. Some techniques give the estimate in <math display="inline">L^p</math> directly, without this loss. For the Couette flow, the explicit solution gives the first estimate of the theorem with <math display="inline">L^p</math> in place of <math display="inline">L^2</math> for every <math display="inline">p\in[1,\infty]</math>, with constants independent of <math display="inline">p</math>.
{{Fold end}}
{{Fold start|kind=idea|title=Idea}}
The key idea underlying all the methods below is that the transport operator <math display="inline">y\partial_x</math> does not commute with the diffusion <math display="inline">\nu\Delta</math>: indeed, <math display="inline">[\Delta,y\partial_x]=2\partial_x\partial_y</math>. If the two commuted, the solution would be <math display="inline">e^{-ty\partial_x}e^{\nu t\Delta}f^{\rm in}</math> and, since the transport preserves the <math display="inline">L^2</math> norm, the flow would have no effect on the decay. We will highlight in each method where this lack of commutation enters.

At first sight, operators that do not commute look like an annoying technical problem. This is a typical instance where a seemingly unfavorable property, looked at in the right way, turns out to be exactly what helps.
{{Fold end}}
== Notation and setting ==
Throughout, <math display="inline">\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}</math>. For the Fourier transform in <math display="inline">x</math> we write
<math display="block">f(t,x,y)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f_k(t,y)e^{ikx},\qquad f_k(t,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{T}}f(t,x,y)e^{-ikx}\,dx,</math>
so that <math display="inline">f_0=\langle f\rangle_x</math> and <math display="inline">\|f\|_{L^2}^2=2\pi\sum_{k}\|f_k\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}^2</math>. Note that in this model each <math display="inline">k</math>-mode evolves independently of the others:
<math display="block">\partial_tf_k+ikyf_k=\nu(\partial_{yy}-k^2)f_k,\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}.</math>

The Sobolev norms in the theorem are <math display="inline">\|g\|_{H^1}^2=\|g\|_{L^2}^2+\|\nabla g\|_{L^2}^2</math> and its dual,
<math display="block">\|g\|_{H^{-1}}=\sup\Big\{\int_{\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}}g\varphi\,dx\,dy\ :\ \|\varphi\|_{H^1}\leq1\Big\}.</math>

== One example, every technique ==
Each proof below is written for this example only, to show the mechanism; the general results, with complete proofs, are in the part ''Techniques and general results''.

{{Fold start|kind=note|title=The estimates mode by mode}}
Since each <math display="inline">k</math>-mode evolves independently, the estimates of the theorem can be stated for each mode separately, keeping track of the dependence on <math display="inline">k</math>. There exist constants <math display="inline">c,C>0</math>, independent of <math display="inline">\nu</math> and <math display="inline">k</math>, such that for all <math display="inline">k\neq0</math> and <math display="inline">t\geq0</math>
<math display="block">\|f_k(t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}\leq Ce^{-c\nu^{1/3}|k|^{2/3}t}\|f_k^{\rm in}\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})},</math>
<math display="block">\|f_k(t)\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb{R})}\leq\frac{C}{1+|k|t}e^{-c\nu^{1/3}|k|^{2/3}t}\|f_k^{\rm in}\|_{H^{1}(\mathbb{R})},</math>
where <math display="inline">H^{\pm1}(\mathbb{R})</math> are the Sobolev norms in <math display="inline">y</math> only. Higher modes are therefore mixed and dissipated faster. The theorem follows by summing over <math display="inline">k\neq0</math>, since <math display="inline">|k|\geq1</math>.
{{Fold end}}

=== Explicit solution ===
{{Proof start|id=proof-couette-explicit|title=Proof by the explicit solution}}
In this proof we take full advantage of the simplicity of the mathematical setting, which is also what allowed Kelvin and Kolmogorov to write down the solution explicitly.

For the equation at mode <math display="inline">k</math>, we can also take the Fourier transform in <math display="inline">y</math>, with the notation
<math display="block">\hat f_k(t,\eta)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_k(t,y)e^{-i\eta y}\,dy,\qquad f_k(t,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\hat f_k(t,\eta)e^{i\eta y}\,d\eta,</math>
so that <math display="inline">\|f\|_{L^2}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\|\hat f_k\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})}^2</math>. By elementary properties of the Fourier transform (multiplication by <math display="inline">y</math> becomes <math display="inline">i\partial_\eta</math>), the equation becomes
<math display="block">\partial_t\hat f_k-k\partial_\eta\hat f_k=-\nu(k^2+\eta^2)\hat f_k.</math>
This is an advection equation in Fourier, with a damping term. We can then follow the characteristics in <math display="inline">\eta</math>, which are the lines <math display="inline">\eta+kt=\text{const}</math>, and deduce that the explicit solution is given by
<math display="block">\hat f_k(t,\eta)=\exp\Big(-\nu\int_0^t\big(k^2+(\eta+k\tau)^2\big)\,d\tau\Big)\,\hat f^{\rm in}_k(\eta+kt).</math>
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=Where the non-commutation enters}}
In Fourier, the transport is the translation <math display="inline">\eta\mapsto\eta+kt</math> and the diffusion is the multiplication by <math display="inline">-\nu(k^2+\eta^2)</math>. The lack of commutation is simply reflected in the fact that the damping is not constant along the characteristics:
<math display="block">\frac{d}{d\tau}\Big[-\big(k^2+(\eta+k\tau)^2\big)\Big]=-2k(\eta+k\tau),</math>
which is exactly the symbol of the commutator <math display="inline">[\Delta,y\partial_x]=2\partial_x\partial_y</math> at the frequency <math display="inline">(k,\eta+k\tau)</math>. If the two operators commuted, the damping would be constant along the characteristics, the integral in the exponent would be trivial, and we would only recover the decay of the heat equation, as in the idea above. Instead, the frequency in <math display="inline">y</math> grows linearly in time along the characteristics, so the damping grows like <math display="inline">\nu k^2\tau^2</math> and its integral like <math display="inline">\nu k^2t^3</math>.
{{Fold end}}
The only thing left is therefore to estimate the integral in the exponent, for which we claim that
<math display="block">\int_0^t\big(k^2+(\eta+k\tau)^2\big)\,d\tau\geq k^2t+\frac{1}{12}k^2t^3\qquad\text{for all }\eta\in\mathbb{R}.</math>
{{Proof start|id=proof-couette-explicit-claim|title=Proof of the claim}}
Computing the integral and completing the square in <math display="inline">\eta</math>,
<math display="block">\int_0^t(\eta+k\tau)^2\,d\tau=\eta^2t+\eta kt^2+\frac{1}{3}k^2t^3=t\Big(\eta+\frac{kt}{2}\Big)^2+\frac{1}{12}k^2t^3\geq\frac{1}{12}k^2t^3,</math>
with equality only for <math display="inline">\eta=-kt/2</math>.
{{Proof end}}
Therefore, using that <math display="inline">f-\langle f\rangle_x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}}f_ke^{ikx}</math>, by Plancherel, the fact that <math display="inline">|k|\geq1</math> and that <math display="inline">\nu t^3\geq3\nu^{1/3}t-2</math>, we get
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}\|(f-\langle f\rangle_x)(t)\|_{L^2}^2&=\sum_{k\neq0}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-2\nu\int_0^t(k^2+(\eta+k\tau)^2)\,d\tau}\,|\hat f^{\rm in}_k(\eta+kt)|^2\,d\eta\\&\leq C^2e^{-2c\nu^{1/3}t}\,\|f^{\rm in}-\langle f^{\rm in}\rangle_x\|_{L^2}^2.\end{aligned}</math>
This proves the desired enhanced dissipation estimate. The constants can be explicitly computed.
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=The constants}}
Indeed, the claim and <math display="inline">|k|\geq1</math> give the more precise bound
<math display="block">\|(f-\langle f\rangle_x)(t)\|_{L^2}^2\leq e^{-2\nu t-\frac{1}{6}\nu t^3}\,\|f^{\rm in}-\langle f^{\rm in}\rangle_x\|_{L^2}^2.</math>
Moreover, <math display="inline">s^3-3s+2=(s-1)^2(s+2)\geq0</math> for <math display="inline">s\geq0</math>, which for <math display="inline">s=\nu^{1/3}t</math> is the inequality <math display="inline">\nu t^3\geq3\nu^{1/3}t-2</math>. Hence <math display="inline">e^{-\frac{1}{6}\nu t^3}\leq e^{\frac{1}{3}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\nu^{1/3}t}</math>, and one can take <math display="inline">c=1/4</math> and <math display="inline">C=e^{1/6}</math>.
{{Fold end}}

For the mixing estimate, one can directly use the characterization of the Sobolev norms in Fourier, namely
<math display="block">\|g\|_{H^{s}}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+k^2+\eta^2)^{s}\,|\hat g_k(\eta)|^2\,d\eta,</math>
which for <math display="inline">s=\pm1</math> are the norms of the theorem. Since <math display="inline">|k|\geq1</math> and <math display="inline">|k|t\leq|\eta|+|\eta+kt|</math>, by Cauchy–Schwarz we have
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}(1+t)^2\leq(1+|k|t)^2&\leq\big(1+|\eta|+|\eta+kt|\big)^2\leq\big(2+\eta^2\big)\big(2+(\eta+kt)^2\big)\\&\leq\big(1+k^2+\eta^2\big)\big(1+k^2+(\eta+kt)^2\big).\end{aligned}</math>
Therefore, bounding the exponential as before,
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}\|(f-\langle f\rangle_x)(t)\|_{H^{-1}}^2&=\sum_{k\neq0}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{-2\nu\int_0^t(k^2+(\eta+k\tau)^2)\,d\tau}}{1+k^2+\eta^2}\,|\hat f^{\rm in}_k(\eta+kt)|^2\,d\eta\\&\leq\frac{C^2e^{-2c\nu^{1/3}t}}{(1+t)^2}\sum_{k\neq0}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(1+k^2+(\eta+kt)^2\big)|\hat f^{\rm in}_k(\eta+kt)|^2\,d\eta\\&=\frac{C^2e^{-2c\nu^{1/3}t}}{(1+t)^2}\,\|f^{\rm in}-\langle f^{\rm in}\rangle_x\|_{H^1}^2,\end{aligned}</math>
which is the mixing estimate.

In fact, the mode-by-mode estimates can be obtained in the same way, by keeping track of <math display="inline">k</math>.
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=The solution in physical space}}
For <math display="inline">\nu>0</math>, inverting the Fourier transform in <math display="inline">y</math> in the explicit solution is a Gaussian integral, which gives
<math display="block">f_k(t,y)=e^{-\nu k^2t-\frac{1}{12}\nu k^2t^3}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\nu t}}\,e^{-\frac{(y-y')^2}{4\nu t}}\,e^{-ikt\frac{y+y'}{2}}f_k^{\rm in}(y')\,dy'.</math>
Summing over <math display="inline">k</math>, by the Poisson summation formula we get
<math display="block">f(t,x,y)=\int_{\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}}G_t(x,y,x',y')f^{\rm in}(x',y')\,dx'dy',</math>
with
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}G_t(x,y,x',y')&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\nu t}}\,e^{-\frac{(y-y')^2}{4\nu t}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_t^2}}\exp\Big(-\frac{\big(x-x'-t\frac{y+y'}{2}+2\pi n\big)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\Big),\\\sigma_t^2&=2\nu t+\frac{1}{6}\nu t^3.\end{aligned}</math>
Without the diffusion in <math display="inline">x</math>, namely with <math display="inline">\sigma_t^2=\frac{1}{6}\nu t^3</math>, and on the whole plane, namely keeping only the term <math display="inline">n=0</math>, this is the fundamental solution written by [[Literature#Kolmogorov1934|Kolmogorov (1934)]]. In the variable <math display="inline">x</math> the solution spreads over the length <math display="inline">\sqrt{\nu t^3}</math>, much larger than the diffusive one <math display="inline">\sqrt{\nu t}</math>. For <math display="inline">t\gg\nu^{-1/3}</math> this length exceeds the size of the torus and the kernel is almost independent of <math display="inline">x</math>: this is the enhanced dissipation seen in physical space.
{{Fold end}}
{{Proof end}}

=== Resolvent method ===
{{Proof start|id=proof-couette-resolvent|title=Proof by the resolvent method}}
We fix <math display="inline">k\neq0</math> and write <math display="inline">f_k=e^{-\nu k^2t}g</math>. Then the function <math display="inline">g</math> solves
<math display="block">\partial_tg+H_kg=0,\qquad H_k:=-\nu\partial_{yy}+iky\quad\text{on }L^2(\mathbb{R}).</math>
We note that the spectrum of <math display="inline">H_k</math> on <math display="inline">L^2(\mathbb{R})</math> is in fact empty (it is a complex Airy operator), and we aim instead at estimating the resolvent of <math display="inline">H_k</math>. To this end, we define the ''pseudospectral abscissa'' of <math display="inline">H_k</math> as
<math display="block">\Psi(H_k):=\inf\big\{\|(H_k-ik\lambda)g\|\ :\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R},\ g\in D(H_k),\ \|g\|=1\big\}.</math>
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=What the pseudospectral abscissa measures}}
For <math display="inline">\varepsilon>0</math>, the <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math>-pseudospectrum of <math display="inline">H_k</math> is the set of <math display="inline">z\in\mathbb{C}</math> where the resolvent is large, <math display="inline">\|(H_k-z)^{-1}\|>1/\varepsilon</math>. Equivalently, it is the set of <math display="inline">z</math> with an approximate eigenfunction, <math display="inline">\|(H_k-z)g\|<\varepsilon\|g\|</math>. For a self-adjoint operator this is the <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math>-neighbourhood of the spectrum. For an operator that is not normal, as <math display="inline">H_k</math>, it can be much larger, and it is the resolvent, not the spectrum, that controls the semigroup. The pseudospectral abscissa is the largest <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math> for which the <math display="inline">\varepsilon</math>-pseudospectrum does not touch the imaginary axis, namely <math display="inline">\Psi(H_k)=\big(\sup_{\lambda}\|(H_k-ik\lambda)^{-1}\|\big)^{-1}</math>. For <math display="inline">H_k</math> a translation in <math display="inline">y</math> only shifts <math display="inline">\operatorname{Im}z</math>, so the pseudospectra are half-planes. For more on pseudospectra, see [[Literature#TrefethenEmbree2005|Trefethen and Embree (2005)]].
{{Fold end}}
This is a fundamental quantity, which controls the decay in time of the semigroups generated by accretive operators (<math display="inline">H</math> is accretive if <math display="inline">-H</math> is dissipative). Indeed, Gearhart–Prüss type bounds link the pseudospectral abscissa to the decay of the semigroup, see [[Literature#HelfferSjostrand2010|Helffer and Sjöstrand (2010)]], and here we appeal to the result of [[Literature#Wei2021Resolvent|Wei (2021)]] (see [[Enhanced-dissipation tools#thm-gearhart-pruss-wei|the Toolkit]]), which tells us that
<math display="block">\|e^{-tH_k}\|_{L^2\to L^2}\leq e^{\pi/2}\,e^{-\Psi(H_k)t}\qquad\text{for all }t\geq0.</math>
Therefore, the enhanced dissipation estimate follows from the claim below.
{{Theorem start|id=clm-couette-resolvent|title=Claim.}}
There exists <math display="inline">c_0>0</math>, independent of <math display="inline">\nu</math> and <math display="inline">k</math>, such that <math display="inline">\Psi(H_k)\geq c_0\,\nu^{1/3}|k|^{2/3}</math>.
{{Theorem end}}
Once the claim is proved, the enhanced dissipation estimate of the theorem follows by going back from <math display="inline">g</math> to <math display="inline">f_k</math> and summing over <math display="inline">|k|\geq1</math>.
{{Proof start|id=proof-clm-couette-resolvent|title=Proof of the claim}}
Fix <math display="inline">\lambda\in\mathbb{R}</math> and <math display="inline">g\in D(H_k)</math>, and let
<math display="block">F_\lambda:=(H_k-ik\lambda)g=-\nu\partial_{yy}g+ik(y-\lambda)g.</math>
The goal is to bound <math display="inline">\|g\|</math> by <math display="inline">\|F_\lambda\|</math>, uniformly in <math display="inline">\lambda</math>.

'''Step 1 (energy identity).''' The first observation is the standard energy identity, which in this spectral picture reads
<math display="block">\operatorname{Re}\big(\langle F_\lambda,g\rangle\big)=\nu\|\partial_yg\|^2,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\nu\|\partial_yg\|^2\leq\|F_\lambda\|\|g\|.</math>
Note that here we have not used the transport operator at all.

'''Step 2 (using the transport).''' To use the transport, we test against <math display="inline">(y-\lambda)g</math> and take the imaginary part. Integrating by parts once,
<math display="block">\operatorname{Im}\big(\langle F_\lambda,(y-\lambda)g\rangle\big)=k\|(y-\lambda)g\|^2+\nu\operatorname{Im}\big(\langle\partial_yg,g\rangle\big),</math>
and therefore
<math display="block">|k|\,\|(y-\lambda)g\|^2\leq\|F_\lambda\|\,\|(y-\lambda)g\|+\nu\|\partial_yg\|\|g\|.</math>
This controls <math display="inline">g</math> away from the critical layer <math display="inline">y=\lambda</math>, where the transport vanishes. To recover the full norm of <math display="inline">g</math> we use a functional inequality, which only requires an integration by parts:
<math display="block">\|g\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_y(y-\lambda)\,|g|^2\,dy=-2\operatorname{Re}\big(\langle(y-\lambda)g,\partial_yg\rangle\big)\leq2\,\|(y-\lambda)g\|\,\|\partial_yg\|.</math>
In words, <math display="inline">g</math> cannot concentrate near the critical layer unless its derivative is large.

'''Step 3 (conclusion).''' By Step 2 and Young's inequality,
<math display="block">\|(y-\lambda)g\|^2\leq\frac{1}{k^2}\|F_\lambda\|^2+\frac{2\nu}{|k|}\|\partial_yg\|\|g\|.</math>
Inserting this in the functional inequality, and using Step 1 to bound <math display="inline">\|\partial_yg\|</math>,
<math display="block">\|g\|^4\leq4\,\|(y-\lambda)g\|^2\|\partial_yg\|^2\lesssim\frac{1}{\nu k^2}\|F_\lambda\|^3\|g\|+\frac{1}{\nu^{1/2}|k|}\|F_\lambda\|^{3/2}\|g\|^{5/2}.</math>
By Young's inequality once more, <math display="inline">\|g\|^3\lesssim\frac{1}{\nu k^2}\|F_\lambda\|^3</math>, that is <math display="inline">\|F_\lambda\|\gtrsim\nu^{1/3}|k|^{2/3}\|g\|</math> uniformly in <math display="inline">\lambda</math>.
{{Fold start|kind=note|title=A more flexible argument: splitting near and away from the critical layer}}
The functional inequality of Step 2 uses that <math display="inline">y-\lambda</math> has derivative one everywhere. For a general shear <math display="inline">v(y)</math> this is not available: for instance <math display="inline">\int v'|g|^2</math> has no sign if <math display="inline">v</math> is not monotone. One then splits the norm of <math display="inline">g</math>, for <math display="inline">\delta>0</math> to be chosen.

''Near the critical layer'' the transport is perturbative and only the dissipation is available, but the region is thin:
<math display="block">\int_{|y-\lambda|<\delta}|g|^2\,dy\leq2\delta\|g\|_{L^\infty}^2\leq2\delta\,\|g\|\,\|\partial_yg\|.</math>
''Away from the critical layer'' the transport can be inverted:
<math display="block">\int_{|y-\lambda|\geq\delta}|g|^2\,dy\leq\frac{1}{\delta^2}\|(y-\lambda)g\|^2\leq\frac{1}{k^2\delta^2}\|F_\lambda\|^2+\frac{2\nu}{|k|\delta^2}\|\partial_yg\|\|g\|.</math>
Adding the two,
<math display="block">\|g\|^2\leq\frac{1}{k^2\delta^2}\|F_\lambda\|^2+2\Big(\delta+\frac{\nu}{|k|\delta^2}\Big)\|\partial_yg\|\|g\|.</math>
The two terms in the bracket balance for <math display="inline">\delta=(\nu/|k|)^{1/3}</math>, the width of the critical layer, and one concludes with Step 1 as before. This is the structure of the proofs for general shear flows, where the test function away from the layer is usually a regularisation of <math display="inline">\operatorname{sgn}(v-\lambda)</math>; see [[Literature#Gallay2022Bourbaki|Gallay (2022)]] and [[Literature#CotiZelatiGallay2023|Coti Zelati and Gallay (2023)]].
{{Fold end}}
{{Proof end}}

'''Uniform mixing estimate.''' It remains to prove the uniform mixing estimate. Here it is convenient to use something that commutes, namely the vector field
<math display="block">Z_k:=\partial_y+ikt.</math>
This is a commuting vector field for the transport equation (namely <math display="inline">[Z_k,\partial_t+iky]=0</math>), but in this particular case it also commutes with the dissipation. Hence <math display="inline">Z_kf_k</math> solves exactly the same equation as <math display="inline">f_k</math>, with datum <math display="inline">\partial_yf_k^{\rm in}</math>, and by the enhanced dissipation estimate
<math display="block">\|(\partial_y+ikt)f_k(t)\|_{L^2}\leq Ce^{-c\nu^{1/3}|k|^{2/3}t}\|\partial_yf_k^{\rm in}\|_{L^2}.</math>
To bound the <math display="inline">H^{-1}</math> norm, we take a test function <math display="inline">\varphi\in H^1(\mathbb{R})</math> and note that, integrating by parts,
<math display="block">ikt\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_k\varphi\,dy=\int_{\mathbb{R}}(Z_kf_k)\varphi\,dy+\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_k\,\partial_y\varphi\,dy.</math>
Therefore, since for <math display="inline">|k|t\leq1</math> there is nothing to prove, by the dual definition of the <math display="inline">H^{-1}</math> norm and the enhanced dissipation estimates for <math display="inline">Z_kf_k</math> and <math display="inline">f_k</math> we conclude that, for <math display="inline">|k|t\geq1</math>,
<math display="block">\|f_k(t)\|_{H^{-1}}\leq\frac{1}{|k|t}\Big(\|Z_kf_k(t)\|_{L^2}+\|f_k(t)\|_{L^2}\Big)\lesssim\frac{1}{1+|k|t}\,e^{-c\nu^{1/3}|k|^{2/3}t}\,\|f_k^{\rm in}\|_{H^1}.</math>
{{Proof end}}
General theory: [[Spectral methods]].
